newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - April 10.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Thursday:
* Procter & Gamble said it would acquire Tambrands for $50 per share or $1.85 billion, in what would be its largest acquisition ever.
* Dow Chemical and General Electric said they resolved a suit in which Dow had accused General Electric of aggressively hiring Dow employees privy to trade secrets.
* Tele-Communications said it would not spin off Liberty Media and two other units into separate companies because it could not get a favorable tax ruling.
* The Dow industrials fell 45.32 points to 6,563.84, dragged down by weakness in financial and technology issues.
* Two Canadian companies, Rogers Cablesystems and Shaw Communications acquired stakes in @Home Network, a company that provides Internet service over cable.
* The chairman of Italy's Fiat, Cesare Romiti, 73, was convicted of having falsified company accounts.

* Moody's Investors Service lowered its long-term credit rating on Thailand, saying its unstable, personality-based coalition governments were ill-suited to addressing the country's financial problems.
* China's inflation rate fell to three percent in the first quarter.
* Italians are concerned about a U.S. law that would require silk textiles finished in Italy to carry a "Made in China" label because the raw silk came from China.
* Wall Street Journal publisher Dow Jones reported a 32.5 percent decline in first quarter earnings, hurt by a decline in operating income at its Telerate financial information unit.
* The Metropolitan Museum of Art is trying to attract several ethnic groups, including Armenians, Greeks, Russians and Ukranians, to build attendance at its "The Glory of Byzantium" exhibit.
* A survey showed the proportion of minority reporters and editors at U.S. newspapers rose slightly last year, but only because total newsroom employment fell.
* Market place: For American investors, the Japanese stock market has hit a four-year low.
* Tensions, caused by industry shakeups and job losses, are growing as Europe moves to a unified market.
